title: Henry VIII
subtitle: The king who broke with Rome in search of a son

package.intro: Henry VIII married six times, executed two of his wives, broke England away from the Church of Rome and closed more than eight hundred monasteries, all in the search for a male heir. This documentary follows the golden young prince who became one of England's most feared kings, and weighs what he left behind.
facts: Born 28 June 1491 at Greenwich, the second son of Henry VII
Became king in April 1509, aged 17, and married Catherine of Aragon that June
Given the title 'Defender of the Faith' by Pope Leo X in 1521
Married Anne Boleyn in January 1533; Elizabeth was born that September
The Act of Supremacy (1534) made the king Supreme Head of the Church of England
Sir Thomas More was executed on 6 July 1535; Anne Boleyn on 19 May 1536
More than 800 religious houses were dissolved between 1536 and 1540
Died at Whitehall on 28 January 1547, aged 55
package.sources: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Historic Royal Palaces, the Mary Rose Trust, J. J. Scarisbrick's Henry VIII, David Starkey's Six Wives, Diarmaid MacCulloch's Thomas Cromwell, Eamon Duffy's The Stripping of the Altars.

sections.name: Cold open

lines.title: HENRY VIII
lines.sub: The king who broke with Rome in search of a son

lines: On the nineteenth of May 1536, inside the Tower of London, a queen of England was executed with a sword. Her husband, the king, had married her only three years earlier.
Anne Boleyn had been convicted of adultery, incest and treason. Most historians believe the charges were false. Eleven days after her death, the king married again.

lines.label: two annulled · two beheaded · one died · one survived

lines: Henry the Eighth married six times. Two marriages were annulled, two wives were beheaded, one died after giving birth, and one outlived him.
He is remembered as a Renaissance prince who remade England's church, and as a tyrant who destroyed anyone in his way. Both are true.

sections.name: The spare
lines: Henry was born at Greenwich in June 1491, the second son of Henry the Seventh, the first Tudor king, who had won his crown on a battlefield six years before.
He was not meant to be king. But in 1502 his elder brother Arthur died, aged fifteen, months after marrying a Spanish princess, Catherine of Aragon.
To keep the alliance with Spain, it was agreed that Henry would one day marry his brother's widow. The pope granted a special dispensation to allow it.

sections.name: The golden prince

lines.name: Henry VIII
lines.role: King at seventeen. Athlete, scholar and musician.

lines: In April 1509 his father died, and Henry became king at seventeen. Within weeks he married Catherine. He was tall, athletic, learned and musical, and foreign ambassadors praised him.
He left much of the work of government to Thomas Wolsey, a butcher's son who rose to be a cardinal and the king's chief minister.
He longed for glory and spent heavily on war with France. In 1513, while he campaigned there, his army at home crushed a Scottish invasion at Flodden, killing the Scottish king.

lines.label: Field of the Cloth of Gold · 1520

lines: In 1520 he met the King of France near Calais at a festival so lavish it became known as the Field of the Cloth of Gold.

lines.head: Defender of the Faith
lines.sub: Pope honours Henry's book against Luther

lines: In 1521 he published a book attacking Martin Luther, and the pope rewarded him with the title Defender of the Faith. British monarchs still use it.

sections.name: The King's Great Matter
lines: Catherine was pregnant at least six times. Only one child survived infancy: a daughter, Mary, born in 1516.

lines.text: No son, he feared, meant civil war.

lines: Henry was desperate for a son. His family's hold on the crown was only one generation old, and England had no tradition of a reigning queen.

lines.name: Anne Boleyn
lines.role: Courtier. Refused to be the king's mistress. Queen, 1533 – 1536.

lines: By 1526 he had fallen for Anne Boleyn, a sharp, well-educated woman at his court. She would not settle for being his mistress.
Henry convinced himself his marriage was cursed, citing a verse in the Book of Leviticus against marrying a brother's wife. He asked the pope to annul it.
The pope, Clement the Seventh, would not do it. He was under the power of Catherine's nephew, the Emperor Charles the Fifth, whose troops had sacked Rome in 1527.
Wolsey failed to get the annulment. He was stripped of power in 1529 and died the next year, on his way to face charges of treason.

sections.name: Break with Rome

lines.name: Thomas Cromwell
lines.role: Lawyer and chief minister. Architect of the break with Rome.

lines: A new chief minister, Thomas Cromwell, found a way out. If the pope would not grant an annulment, England would stop obeying the pope.
Henry secretly married Anne in January 1533. His new Archbishop of Canterbury, Thomas Cranmer, declared the first marriage void. In September, Anne gave birth to a daughter, Elizabeth.
In 1534, Parliament's Act of Supremacy declared the king Supreme Head of the Church of England.

lines.text: Words alone could now be treason.

lines: A new Treasons Act made it a capital crime even to call the king a heretic or a tyrant.

lines.label: Sir Thomas More · Tower of London · 1535

lines: Henry's former Lord Chancellor, the scholar Sir Thomas More, refused to swear the oath the new order demanded. He was executed in July 1535, weeks after Bishop John Fisher.

sections.name: The terror
lines: Cromwell then turned to the Church's wealth. Between 1536 and 1540, more than eight hundred monasteries, nunneries and friaries were closed, and their lands taken by the crown.
Thousands of monks, nuns and friars were turned out. Libraries, shrines and centuries of art were destroyed, and most of the land was sold to nobles and gentry.
In 1536, tens of thousands in the north rose in protest, in the Pilgrimage of Grace. Henry promised pardons and a hearing. After further unrest, around two hundred people were executed.
Catherine of Aragon, banished from court, died in January 1536, still insisting she was Henry's true wife.
Anne, too, had failed to produce a living son. Within months she was accused of adultery with five men, one of them her own brother. All of them were executed.

lines.label: between Prince Edward's birth and his mother's death

lines: Henry married Jane Seymour eleven days after Anne's death. In October 1537 she gave him the son he wanted, Edward. Twelve days later, she died.

sections.name: The later wives

lines.head: Cromwell executed
lines.sub: After the king's fourth marriage fails

lines: His fourth marriage, to a German princess, Anne of Cleves, was annulled after six months. Henry blamed Cromwell, who had arranged it, and had him executed.
That same day, Henry married Catherine Howard, still a teenager. Eighteen months later, she was executed for adultery.

lines.name: Henry VIII
lines.role: Obese, in pain, and increasingly suspicious.

lines: By now Henry was hugely overweight, with a painful ulcerated leg. A heavy fall while jousting in 1536 may have made it worse. Some historians think that fall changed him. Others say the cruelty was always there.
His sixth wife, Catherine Parr, a widow and a published religious writer, outlived him.

sections.name: The last years
lines: He spent his last years at war with France and Scotland. To pay for it, he sold off monastery lands and debased the coinage, mixing cheaper metal into the silver.
He also built up the navy. In 1545 he watched from the shore as his warship, the Mary Rose, sank in the Solent with most of her crew.
The killing went on to the end. Days before Henry died, the young poet Henry Howard, Earl of Surrey, was executed for treason.
Henry died at Whitehall on the twenty-eighth of January 1547, aged fifty-five. His nine-year-old son became Edward the Sixth.

sections.name: Legacy
lines: All three of his surviving children reigned. Edward pushed England further towards Protestantism. Mary, Catherine's daughter, tried to restore Catholicism, and nearly three hundred Protestants were burned. Then came Elizabeth.

lines.text: Two wives, two of his closest ministers and hundreds of others went to their deaths.
lines.who: summary of the case against Henry

lines: Critics see a vain, cruel king who executed two wives, two of his closest ministers and hundreds of others, poured his father's fortune into wars, and destroyed centuries of monastic heritage.

lines.head: What he left behind
items: Wales joined to England in law

lines: Defenders point to what lasted: a national church, a Parliament strengthened by the laws it passed for him, a larger navy, and the union of Wales with England in law.

lines.text: He wanted a son. History remembers his daughter.

lines: Henry tore England away from Rome, and married and discarded wife after wife, in his search for a male heir.
His son died at fifteen. The daughter he had declared illegitimate, Elizabeth, became one of the most celebrated monarchs England ever had.
